meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The idea is not to live forever, it is to create something that will'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Warhol. The line rewrites a sentence from Chuck Palahniuk's 2003 novel Diary, published sixteen years after Warhol's death. Sources checked and shown.

answer.label: Not Andy Warhol — actually Chuck Palahniuk
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is documented in Chuck Palahniuk’s novel Diary (Doubleday, 2003), where the character Grace Wilmot says it to her daughter-in-law Misty: “We all die… The goal isn’t to live forever, the goal is to create something that will.” The smoother “The idea is not to live forever…” wording that travels under Warhol’s name is a later rewrite — and no Warhol source has ever been produced for it. Warhol died in 1987, sixteen years before the novel was published.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually appears

docMeta.dd: Grace Wilmot, measuring her daughter-in-law Misty
A later rewrite, re-credited to Andy Warhol

source.excerpt: …suicide attempts, he died at thirty-two. Grace says, “We all die.” She says, “The goal isn’t to live forever, the goal is to create something that will.” She runs the tape measure down the length of Misty’s legs…
trail: Wikiquote’s Andy Warhol page ↗ collects his sourced remarks decade by decade, from the 1960s through the 1980s. This sentence is not on it — not in the sourced sections, not among the undated lines, nowhere.

Running the phrase through the Internet Archive’s scanned-book index via Open Library ↗ returns it inside three separate scanned editions of Palahniuk’s Diary, in the same passage each time. Wikiquote’s page for the novel ↗ lists the line and names Grace as the speaker.

Every printed appearance of the Warhol-credited rewrite that the same index turns up ↗ is a later compilation. The earliest I could locate is Charlotte Lowe’s fact-o-pedia ↗ (HarperCollins, 2009) — six years after the novel, and filed under “Warhol, Andy.”

Princeton University Press, introducing its sourced collection Warhol-isms ↗ (2022), puts the problem plainly: Warhol “is so quotable that things he never said are endlessly and plausibly attributed to him.” The book exists to separate the real lines from exactly this kind of drift.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Internet Archive’s full-text scan of the Doubleday edition, reached through Open Library’s search-inside index. The leading and trailing ellipses are the snippet boundaries, not the novel’s punctuation; the passage returns identically from three separately scanned copies of the book.

source.rightsNote: The only work this sentence can actually be traced to is Diary: A Novel, published by Doubleday in New York on 26 August 2003 — comfortably inside US copyright, with decades left to run. The popular Warhol-credited rewording has no separate documented source of its own, so it inherits the status of the text it derives from rather than gaining any claim to the public domain.

author.name: Chuck Palahniuk
author.kicker: The writer who actually wrote it
author.heading: Chuck Palahniuk
author.bio: Chuck Palahniuk, born in Pasco, Washington in 1962, is an American novelist known for spare, transgressive fiction with a taste for the grotesque. His debut Fight Club (1996) became a cultural landmark after its 1999 film adaptation, followed by Invisible Monsters (1999) and Choke (2001). Diary (2003) is a horror-tinged novel about a painter consumed by the island community that needs her work — the setting in which the sentence now credited to Warhol was actually written.

Spoken by the character Grace Wilmot; wording confirmed against the Internet Archive's full-text scans of three editions. copyAttribution: "The idea is not to live forever, it is to create something that will" is not Andy Warhol's. It is a rewrite of a line from Chuck Palahniuk's novel Diary (New York: Doubleday, 2003), where the character Grace says: "We all die… The goal isn't to live forever, the goal is to create something that will." Warhol died in 1987, sixteen years before the novel was published, and no Warhol source for the quote has ever been produced. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How Warhol got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook Warhol fake: a tidy, gallery-friendly aphorism about art outlasting the artist, welded to the name of the artist most associated with fame and permanence. The wording is not his, and the sentence it was rewritten from was published sixteen years after he died.

items.why: Not one citation has ever been offered — no interview, no book, no film. Wikiquote’s Andy Warhol page ↗ does not carry it in any section, and Princeton University Press notes that Warhol “is so quotable that things he never said are endlessly and plausibly attributed to him” in its overview of Warhol-isms ↗.

items.scope: A likely route for the mix-up
items.who: Two books called some version of ‘Diary’
items.why: Palahniuk’s novel is titled Diary. Warhol’s own posthumous book, listed on his Wikipedia entry ↗, is The Andy Warhol Diaries (1989). A quotation filed only as “from Diary” is one careless step from being re-filed under Warhol — this is our own reading of the coincidence, not a documented chain of custody.

items.who: Trivia books, art titles, classroom guides
items.why: Searching the Internet Archive’s scanned books for the Warhol wording ↗ returns only post-2003 compilations — a 2009 HarperCollins trivia book, a poetry collection, a classroom creativity guide, and a popular history of Warhol’s 1963 road trip — every one of them crediting Warhol and none citing where he supposedly said it.

items.who: Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes and the rest
items.why: The same thought circulates under two names at once: user-contributed pages carry it as Warhol with no source at all ↗ and, in its original wording, as Palahniuk with the book named ↗. Only one of those two has a book behind it.

misattribution.truthLine: What Palahniuk actually wrote, in Diary (2003) ↗, is a character’s line, not an artist’s manifesto: Grace says, “We all die.” She says, “The goal isn’t to live forever, the goal is to create something that will.”

context.heading: Why the wrong name sticks
lead: The line works better as Warhol than as Palahniuk, and that is precisely the problem. Warhol is the artist of the reproducible image — the soup can, the silkscreen, the thing that outlives the hand that made it — so an epigram about creating something that survives you slides onto his name without friction. Nobody stops to ask for a citation, because it already sounds like something he would have said.

In the novel the sentence lands very differently. Grace Wilmot is measuring her daughter-in-law for a dress, having just recounted an artist’s early death, and the comfort she offers is chilly rather than uplifting — part of a plot in which a community deliberately consumes an artist to produce work it can sell. Lifted out of that scene and re-credited to a Pop artist, a sinister line becomes a motivational poster.
detailsBody: Diary was published by Doubleday on 26 August 2003. Warhol died on 22 February 1987. Whatever the sentence is, it is not a remark he made and someone later wrote down.

Warhol’s most famous line — the one about fifteen minutes of fame — is itself widely regarded as a fake, which is the case Princeton University Press leads with when explaining why a sourced collection of his quotations was needed at all. A page like this one exists for the same reason: with Warhol, the burden of proof belongs on the attribution, not on the doubt.
context.pull: Warhol is so quotable that things he never said keep finding their way to him.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Andy Warhol page contains no quote matching "The idea is not to live forever, it is to create something that will" in any section.
Wikipedia's Andy Warhol article gives his birth date as 6 August 1928 and death as 22 February 1987, and lists The Andy Warhol Diaries (1989) among his books.
Wikiquote's Diary (novel) page carries "The goal isn't to live forever, the goal is to create something that will" and attributes it to the character Grace in Chuck Palahniuk's 2003 novel.
Wikipedia's Diary (novel) article gives publication as Doubleday, 26 August 2003, and identifies Grace Wilmot as a character, Misty Wilmot's mother-in-law.

Open Library's search-inside index returns, from three separately scanned editions of Palahniuk's Diary, the passage: "...suicide attempts, he died at thirty-two. Grace says, 'We all die.' She says, 'The goal isn't to live forever, the goal is to create something that will.'"

Open Library's search-inside index returns the Warhol-credited wording only from later compilations (a HarperCollins trivia book, E. Ethelbert Miller's collected poems, a classroom creativity guide, and Deborah Davis's book on Warhol's road trip), with no occurrence predating 2003.
The Internet Archive's catalogue record for Diary: a novel gives Chuck Palahniuk, Doubleday, New York, 2003.

The Internet Archive's catalogue record for The utterly, completely, and totally useless fact-o-pedia gives Charlotte Lowe, HarperCollins Publishers, London, 2009 — the earliest located print appearance crediting the wording to Warhol.

Princeton University Press's overview of Warhol-isms (2022, ed. Larry Warsh) states that Warhol "is so quotable that things he never said are endlessly and plausibly attributed to him" and that the book "separates legend from fact."
Goodreads carries "The idea is not to live forever, it is to create something that will" credited to Andy Warhol with no source given.
Goodreads carries "Grace says, 'We all die.' She says, 'The goal isn't to live forever, the goal is to create something that will.'" credited to Chuck Palahniuk, Diary.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation — a site search for "create something that will" returns "Nothing Found".
Wikipedia's Chuck Palahniuk article gives his birth as 21 February 1962 in Pasco, Washington, and lists Fight Club (1996), Invisible Monsters (1999) and Choke (2001).
